newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia hardliners free Banja Luka police chief.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia hardliners free Banja Luka police chief.

text.p: The newly appointed police chief of Banja Luka was arrested by hardline Bosnian Serb state security men on Tuesday but released after refusing their demands he resign, a senior policeman said.

"Milan Sutilovic was ordered to sign a document on his own suspension which Sutilovic refused to do and, after being held for 30 minutes, he was released," new acting head of state security in Banja Luka Predrag Ceranic told Reuters.
Both Sutilovic and Ceranic are loyal to Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic who is locked in a power struggle with former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Ceranic said Sutilovic was arrested by two policemen with sniper rifles early on Tuesday while leaving the police building and was taken to the sacked Banja Luka police commander Stojan Davidovic who ordered him to resign.

Sutilovic was appointed chief of Banja Luka police after Plavsic's security forces took over the local police station on Sunday. The takeover revealed the station had been used to tap her phone and fax as well as those of hundreds of other officials in this northwestern Bosnian Serb town.

International police said they were investigating allegations that Bosnian Serb nationalist hardliners had intimidated court judges and conducted widespread telephone tapping in their power struggle against Plavsic.
Tuesday's incident reflected mounting tensions in Bosnia's Serb-run areas as Karadzic loyalists sought to shore up their position against their rivals based in Banja Luka.
Plavsic has accused Karadzic and his hardline nationalist allies of rampant corruption and of damaging Serb interests by blocking the peace process.

NATO deployed British peacekeeping troops in Banja Luka after Sunday's takeover of the police station to prevent possible clashes between the rival factions. Plavsic's special police eventually agreed to withdraw from the station under NATO escort and police loyal to Karadzic moved back in.
NATO-led peace force spokesman Major John Blakeley said British troops had dismantled "a number" of roadblocks around the police building which had been set up by Karadzic's police.

Plavsic vowed on Monday to press for early elections to the hardline-dominated Bosnian Serb parliament, despite an adverse court ruling last week, and to carry on fighting what she called "terror" led by Karadzic's allies.
The International Police Task Force (IPTF) said it was sifting through "bags of evidence" taken from the Banja Luka police station.
"We have collected a sizeable quantity of evidence that is now being compiled and recorded," IPTF spokesman Alun Roberts said late on Monday in Banja Luka.

Western officials said IPTF monitors found numerous tapes and transcripts, part of an elaborate eavesdropping operation by hardliners loyal to Karadzic, the wartime Bosnian Serb leader now sought by prosecutors at the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
In Washington, the United States said on Monday it rejected the Bosnian Serb constitutional court's ruling that Plavsic could not call early elections.
The Bosnian Serb cabinet, loyal to Karadzic, accuses Plavsic of being a pawn of foreign enemies allegedly plotting to divide the Serb nation.
